title: How Pune CP's Night Patrolling Initiative Reduced Chain Snatching by 40%
author: Sadrakshan.AI Editorial
excerpt: Pune Commissionerate deployed a structured beat patrolling model across 12 divisions in late 2025. Within four months, chain snatching incidents dropped by over 40%. Here is what they did differently.
body:
Chain snatching had become a serious concern across Pune city through 2024 and early 2025. The incidents were concentrated in specific corridors — mostly areas with dense evening foot traffic near markets, temples, and bus stands.

Instead of adding more officers to the streets randomly, Pune CP's office did something methodical: they mapped the last 18 months of chain snatching FIRs by time, location, and day of week. The data showed clear clusters — 73% of incidents happened between 6:30 PM and 9:00 PM, and 60% of those were within a 2-kilometre radius of just four major intersections.

What Changed

The initiative deployed plain-clothes constables on motorcycles in pairs within these identified hotspots — specifically during the peak window. Regular uniform patrolling continued as before, but the plainclothes deployment was the addition that made the difference.

Officers were rotated weekly so that offenders could not identify them. Nakabandis (vehicle checkpoints) were set up at exit routes from the hot zones, timed to coincide with the historical snatching window.

The Results

Within four months, chain snatching reports in the covered zones dropped by 43%. Neighbouring zones without the intervention saw no significant change, which confirmed that the reduction was caused by the patrolling model rather than seasonal variation.

Nine accused were arrested during this period — all through on-the-spot interception by the plainclothes teams, not through investigation after the fact.

What Other Commissionerates Can Take From This

The method works because it is evidence-based. The starting point was not assumptions about crime — it was actual FIR data mapped carefully. Any district or commissionerate can replicate this by pulling their own data and finding their own clusters before deploying resources.

The Pune CP's office has shared its internal analysis template with the State Crime Records Bureau. Districts can request it through their range DIG offices.

title: Sessions Court Acquittal: Why Witness Statements Collapsed in a 2019 Assault Case — and What the IO Should Have Done
author: Sadrakshan.AI Editorial
excerpt: A case from Buldhana district — prosecuted under Sections 323 and 325 IPC — ended in acquittal at Sessions Court after three key witnesses turned hostile. A close look at what went wrong from the investigation side.
body:
This analysis is based on a Sessions Court judgment from Buldhana district, decided in early 2026. The names of accused, complainant, and witnesses have been withheld. The facts are drawn from the judgment record.

The case: A dispute over agricultural land turned violent. The complainant suffered fractures on both arms. Three independent witnesses were present at the scene. All three gave statements to the IO under Section 161 CrPC within 24 hours of the incident.

What Went Wrong at Trial

By the time the case reached Sessions Court nearly four years later, all three independent witnesses turned hostile. The court noted that their trial statements were contradictory to their earlier 161 statements on material points — not minor details, but the central question of who assaulted whom.

The prosecution tried to cross-examine its own witnesses through the Additional PP, but without corroborating evidence to use as confrontation material, the exercise was limited.

The accused were acquitted.

What the Investigation Lacked

Reading the judgment, three gaps stand out clearly:

  1. No video of the scene: The IO did not record a spot panchanama video. At the time of the offence, every officer had a phone capable of recording. A 2-minute video of the spot — blood marks, location of parties, distance between them — would have been independent, non-hostilisable evidence.
  2. Medical evidence was incomplete: The injury certificate was obtained, but no attempt was made to obtain the treating doctor's statement under Section 161 at the time. The doctor's opinion on the age and nature of fractures was never on record.
  3. Witnesses were not interviewed separately: All three witnesses were at the police station at the same time and gave statements in proximity of each other. The court observed this in its judgment. When witnesses are aware of each other's statements, the independence of those statements is compromised.

For Investigating Officers

Witness hostility is often treated as an external problem — something the IO cannot control. That framing is incorrect. The IO's job is to create an investigation that is robust even when witnesses turn hostile. That means building non-witness evidence from Day 1: video, medical opinion, FSL reports, and careful panchanama documentation.

If the only pillars holding up a prosecution are human witnesses, any one of them turning hostile can bring the whole structure down.

title: If Someone Files a False FIR Against You: What the Law Actually Says
author: Sadrakshan.AI Editorial
excerpt: A false FIR is frightening — especially if you have no experience with the criminal justice system. This article explains exactly what options you have, what the police are required to do, and how courts can protect you.
body:
If you have just found out that an FIR has been registered against you — or you suspect one is about to be — the first reaction is usually panic. The system feels enormous and you feel alone in it.

This article is meant to give you a clear, factual picture of your rights and options. It is not legal advice. For your specific situation, speak to a lawyer. But understanding the law will help you have a better conversation with that lawyer and with the police.

What Is a False FIR?

A First Information Report (FIR) is a document that records the first complaint of a cognisable offence. Anyone can walk into a police station and file an FIR. The police are not permitted to investigate whether the complaint is true before registering it — they are required by law to register it first.

This means that a false complaint can become an FIR quite easily. This is also why the law provides several remedies against false FIRs.

Your Rights the Moment an FIR Is Filed

  • Right to get a copy of the FIR: Under Section 173(2) BNSS (earlier Section 207 CrPC), you are entitled to a free copy of the FIR. The police must give it to you. If they refuse, you can complain to a senior officer.
  • Right to anticipatory bail: If you fear arrest, you can apply for anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS (earlier Section 438 CrPC) before a Sessions Court or High Court. If granted, you cannot be arrested without the court's permission.
  • Right to know the charges: You must be told exactly which sections of the law apply to the FIR against you.

How Can You Challenge a False FIR?

Option 1 — Approach the High Court under Section 528 BNSS (earlier Section 482 CrPC): The High Court has inherent powers to quash an FIR if it is found to be false, frivolous, or an abuse of the process of law. This is the most direct remedy. You file a petition, the court calls for the FIR and related documents, and can stay the investigation in the meantime.

Option 2 — Complain to senior police officers: If you believe the FIR is a fabrication and can show clear evidence of that, a Superintendent of Police or Deputy Commissioner of Police has the authority to direct a fair investigation — or in some cases, recommend closure if the complaint is clearly false.

Option 3 — File a complaint against the false complainant: Filing a false FIR is itself an offence under Section 211 IPC (now BNS equivalent) — making a false charge with intent to injure. Once the original case concludes in your favour, you can initiate proceedings against the person who filed falsely.

What the Police Must Do

The police are required to investigate an FIR fairly — that means they must look at evidence on both sides. They are not supposed to arrest simply because an FIR exists. Arrest requires the IO to be satisfied, based on investigation, that there is sufficient reason to arrest. Many FIRs are investigated and closed without any arrest being made.

If you cooperate with the investigation, provide your version clearly, and engage a lawyer early, the system generally has ways to protect innocent people — even if those protections require effort to access.

Important Note

Every situation is different. The sections of law mentioned here refer to BNSS 2023, which replaced CrPC across India from July 2024. If your case was filed before July 2024, the old CrPC provisions may apply. Your lawyer will know which version applies to your case.
